title: Rural Hospitals Theorem
body_html:
Rural Hospitals Theorem

Theorem (Roth 1986, McVitie-Wilson 1970 for one-to-one). In a finite one-to-one matching market $(M, W, \succ)$, the set of matched participants is invariant across all stable matchings:

$$\{ i \in M : \mu(i) \ne \bot \} = \{ i \in M : \mu'(i) \ne \bot \}$$

for any two stable matchings $\mu, \mu'$ (and symmetrically for $W$).

In particular, the man-proposing optimal $\mu^M$ and the woman-proposing optimal $\mu^W$ match exactly the same individuals.
proof_html:
Sketch

Suppose $\mu, \mu'$ are stable and some man $i$ is matched in $\mu$ but unmatched in $\mu'$. Let $j = \mu(i)$. By [[lattice]], we can WLOG take $\mu = \mu^M$ (men-optimal) and $\mu' = \mu^W$ (women-optimal). Since $\mu(i) = j$ and $\mu^W$ ranks weakly below $\mu^M$ for every man, every man who is matched in $\mu^M$ is also matched in $\mu^W$ (he might be matched to a different — and weakly worse — partner, but he is matched).

Hence the matched-man sets coincide. By symmetry (cardinality of matched participants is the same on both sides), the matched-woman sets coincide too.

Why "Rural Hospitals"?

The name comes from the many-to-one (residency matching) version, where the result says: any hospital that fills fewer positions than its quota under one stable assignment fills exactly the same set of positions (with the same set of residents!) under every stable assignment. Rural hospitals that historically struggled to fill positions still struggle — no mechanism design can rescue them within the stable-matching framework.

The one-to-one version above is the simpler specialization.

Lean Status

To be formalized in MT-L2 (#204). Depends on the lattice structure ([[lattice]]) and proposing-optimality ([[proposing_optimal]]).

References

  • [MSZ Ch.22, Thm 22.14] Maschler, Solan, Zamir, Game Theory.
  • McVitie & Wilson (1970), Stable Marriage Assignment for Unequal Sets.
  • Roth (1986), On the Allocation of Residents to Rural Hospitals. Econometrica 54.
  • Roth & Sotomayor (1990), Ch. 2 §2.4.
